steps.say: Not every prostate cancer needs the knife. Low risk disease, meaning ISUP Grade Group 1 with PSA below 10 and a small cT1c to cT2a tumour, is safely watched rather than treated. Active surveillance tracks the cancer with serial PSA blood tests, multiparametric MRI scans, and protocol repeat biopsies, and only one man in three ever needs treatment later.
steps.tx: Choose **active surveillance** (planned watching with curative intent) as the preferred strategy for **low-risk prostate cancer** (ISUP Grade Group 1, PSA **<10 ng/mL**, stage **cT1c-cT2a**), using serial PSA, **mpMRI** (multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging), and protocol biopsies. Surveillance cures by selection: tumours that stay quiet keep their prostate, while the minority that upgrade receive delayed surgery or radiation with outcomes matching immediate treatment.

vis.alt: Diagram comparing normal prostate with benign prostatic hyperplasia anatomy zones.
vis.caption: Prostate zonal anatomy: low risk tumours under surveillance stay confined to the gland. Credit: bank image.

steps.say: When surgery is chosen, the robot gives the steadiest hands. Robotic assisted radical prostatectomy removes the whole gland through keyholes while peeling the neurovascular bundles, the twin nerve ribbons driving erections, off the prostate between the prostatic fascia and the levator fascia. This nerve sparing plane preserves potency in suitable men without leaving cancer at the margin.
steps.tx: Offer **RARP** (robotic keyhole prostate removal, robotic-assisted radical prostatectomy) with **nerve-sparing** (potency preserving dissection) technique, freeing the **neurovascular bundles** (erection nerve ribbons) between the prostatic fascia and levator fascia. The plane sits outside the tumour but inside the nerves, so margins stay clear while erectile function survives in well selected men with localised disease.

steps.say: After surgery the PSA should fall to zero and stay there, so any confirmed climb is bad news with a precise name. Biochemical recurrence after prostatectomy means two consecutive PSA rises reaching or crossing zero point two nanograms per millilitre. After radiation the bar sits higher because the gland remains: the Phoenix criteria call recurrence a rise of two point zero or more above the lowest post treatment value, the nadir.
steps.tx: Define **biochemical recurrence** (PSA only relapse) after prostatectomy as two consecutive **prostatectomy PSA rise** readings of **0.2 ng/mL** (zero point two) or greater, and after radiation by the **Phoenix criteria** (nadir plus two rule) as a rise of **2.0 ng/mL** (two point zero) or more above the post-treatment **radiation nadir** (lowest PSA after radiotherapy). The lower surgical bar reflects an absent gland, while the higher radiation bar forgives the retained prostate.

steps.say: When PSA creeps up but scans stay blank, PSMA PET finds the hideout. The 68Ga PSMA or 18F PSMA PET CT scan lights up prostate cancer cells through their surface PSMA protein, and it beats every conventional scan at very low PSA values, localising disease even between zero point two and one point zero nanograms per millilitre. A positive spot directs salvage radiation to the target instead of the whole pelvis.
steps.tx: Localise early relapse with **PSMA PET-CT** (prostate protein tracer scan), using **68Ga-PSMA** (gallium tracer) or 18F-PSMA (fluorine tracer) to expose recurrence at PSA levels between **0.2 and 1.0 ng/mL** (zero point two to one), where CT and bone scans stay blind. PSMA avidity maps oligometastatic spots for targeted salvage, so order it at the first confirmed PSA climb rather than waiting for conventional imaging to turn positive.

rows: CT and bone scan at low PSA

steps.say: Starving the cancer of testosterone remains the backbone of advanced treatment. Androgen deprivation therapy is used to drive testosterone down to castrate level, below 50 nanograms per decilitre or one point seven nanomoles per litre, using LHRH agonists like leuprolide, LHRH antagonists like degarelix and relugolix, or the surgical option of removing both testicles. Antagonists are preferred when the fastest testosterone drop with no initial flare is needed, as in painful bony disease.
steps.tx: Start **androgen deprivation therapy** (testosterone starving treatment, ADT) to reach **castrate level** (testosterone **<50 ng/dL**, under fifty, or **<1.7 nmol/L**) with LHRH agonists (**leuprolide**, monthly depot shot), LHRH antagonists (**degarelix**, **relugolix**, faster drop without flare), or bilateral orchiectomy (surgical castration). Pick antagonists for impending cord compression or severe bone pain, and agonists or surgery for steady long term control.

vis.alt: Overview diagram of late onset hypogonadism and the male androgen axis suppression.
vis.caption: Androgen axis suppression: ADT drives testosterone below castrate level. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Metastatic disease that still answers to hormones is now treated with combination attack from day one. The standard for metastatic hormone sensitive cancer is doublet or triplet therapy: ADT plus androgen receptor signalling inhibitors such as enzalutamide, apalutamide, or abiraterone, with docetaxel chemotherapy added for high volume disease. Triplets extend life by years over ADT alone, so single drug castration is now undertreatment.
steps.tx: Treat **mHSPC** (metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer) with doublet or triplet therapy: ADT plus **androgen receptor signaling inhibitors** (**enzalutamide**, **apalutamide**, **abiraterone**) with or without **docetaxel** (taxane chemotherapy) for high volume spread. Combinations delay castration resistance by years, so refer fit metastatic patients for intensified therapy at diagnosis rather than settling for ADT alone.

steps.say: When the cancer outsmarts hormones, its DNA repair defects become its weakness. Metastatic castration resistant cancers carrying homologous recombination repair mutations, most famously BRCA1 and BRCA2, melt under PARP inhibitors such as olaparib and rucaparib, which trap the tumour in its own broken DNA. Testing every advanced patient for HRR mutations is therefore treatment, not curiosity.
steps.tx: Test every **mCRPC** (metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer) for **HRR mutations** (DNA repair defects, homologous recombination repair: **BRCA1/2**), because **PARP inhibitors** (**olaparib**, **rucaparib**) deliver profound responses in mutated tumours. PARP blockade turns broken repair lethal, so a positive BRCA result reroutes the patient from blind chemotherapy to targeted tablets with superior survival.
